title: Environmental detection of the amphibian chytrid fungus in water bodies is associated with host infection along a deforestation gradient
abstract: Abstract Many wildlife pathogens can persist in the environment independently of their hosts, with the habitat itself serving as a reservoir and potential source of transmission. However, reliably detecting and quantifying free‐living pathogen stages across heterogeneous landscapes using environmental DNA methods remains challenging. Understanding how landcover and habitat structure drive pathogen distribution at the environmental and host levels is critical for advancing disease surveillance and ecology. Amphibian chytridiomycosis, caused by the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis ( Bd ), provides a useful model system to address these broader challenges, yet most studies have focused on host–pathogen interactions, with less emphasis on Bd within environmental reservoirs. Using Bd as a model system, we investigated whether pathogen distribution in natural aquatic environments is associated with host infection patterns across gradients of habitat loss. We sampled four tropical amphibian species across eight rainforest landscapes and quantified Bd in paired water and host samples using a high‐capacity water filtration method coupled with digital and real‐time quantitative polymerase chain reaction detection assays. Our results revealed a strong positive correlation between Bd DNA concentrations in water and infection loads on amphibian skin, indicating that environmental Bd DNA is associated with host infection patterns. Forest cover and habitat split (i.e. spatial separation between forests and aquatic breeding sites) were the primary predictors of Bd occurrence, concentration and infection load across environmental and host‐associated forms, and both Bd ‐GPL and Bd ‐Asia‐2/Brazil lineages were detected across our study landscapes. Our study introduces and validates a robust protocol for detecting environmental Bd , providing a scalable approach to quantify pathogen–environment associations across multiple landscapes and environmental gradients. Synthesis and applications : Linking environmental pathogen detection with host infection patterns can improve surveillance of diseases involving environmental transmission, particularly where direct host sampling is logistically challenging. This approach enables the identification of areas of elevated transmission risk and supports targeted monitoring and management under habitat loss and degradation. It also provides a practical tool to guide conservation actions in landscapes undergoing rapid land‐use change.
authors: Ananda Brito de Assis, David Rodriguez, Wesley J. Neely, Carla Martins Lopes, Paula R. Prist, Carlos Arturo Navas, Renato A. Martins, Shannon Buttimer, Célio Fernando Baptista Haddad, C. Guilherme Becker

title: Growth, mortality and regeneration responses to ecological forestry treatments are shaped by local factors, species, and initial treatment impact
abstract: Abstract Ecological forestry rooted in natural disturbance‐based silviculture (NDBS) aims to help maintain or facilitate recovery of ecosystem structure and function toward conditions found in unharvested stands. In the short term, leaving a portion of a stand's merchantable trees intact at harvest should increase similarity in composition and function relative to stands following non‐stand‐replacing natural disturbances such as low‐intensity fires, windthrow, or insect outbreaks and thus maintain biodiversity and other ecosystem services. Testing NDBS requires long‐term data, while assessing the generality of responses to NDBS requires such data from multiple experiments across diverse stand and site conditions. To date, our understanding of forest responses to NDBS has been limited by a lack of opportunities to explore responses across time. In this study, we utilized data from three long‐term experiments encompassing 21 combinations of harvest treatments by stand type plus unharvested reference stands. These experiments provide data to assess responses for 12 to 20 years post‐treatment. We quantified the direction (increasing or decreasing), duration (persisting or transient), magnitude, and temporal dynamics of responses in stand‐level tree growth, mortality, and regeneration abundances. High‐intensity treatments (≥40%) produced strong initial impacts, particularly increased tree mortality (although not statistically significant across all treatments), which in turn had prolonged effects on stand‐level growth through reduced tree density. These treatments also promoted increased broadleaf regeneration, likely due to greater canopy opening and enhanced light availability. We observed an inconsistent stand‐level growth response to treatments, with some treatments showing initial decline while others eventually resulted in higher growth in harvested stands. In mixed stands, coniferous species showed growth benefits when coexisting with broadleaf species, possibly due to reduced intraspecific competition or improved access to resources mediated by broadleaf neighbours. This growth advantage was not observed for broadleaf species, indicating asymmetric benefits in mixed stands. Response patterns and magnitude vary over time and are influenced by local factors such as stand type, overstory retention, species, and initial treatment impact. This variability highlights the potential for tailoring NDBS approaches locally to achieve desired outcomes and underscores the need to incorporate stand‐specific conditions into ecological forestry practices.
authors: Arun K. Bose, Suzanne Brais, K. David Coates, Brian D. Harvey, Richard Kabzems, Rongzhou Man, Charles Nock, Kevin A. Solarik, Manuella Strukelj, S. Ellen Macdonald

title: Same forest, different story: Beetle community responses to non‐native tree species depend on the vertical stratum
abstract: Abstract Increased forest diebacks under climate change necessitate adaptation strategies of forest management, which often include the use of drought‐resistant non‐native tree species. However, their planting has raised concerns about the ecological impacts on forest biodiversity and functioning. Relevant studies are largely limited to single forest strata, often focusing on ground or subcanopy communities, which prevents a comprehensive understanding of how biodiversity responds to changes in native and non‐native tree species identity and composition across forest strata. Here, we provide a synthesis of how the introduction of North American Douglas fir alters different facets of biodiversity across vertical strata in Central European forests. We focused on beetles, a hyperdiverse group of forest biota, and considered economically important stand types including and excluding Douglas fir, namely, monocultures and mixtures of native European beech, native Norway spruce planted outside its natural range and non‐native Douglas fir. Beetle diversity varied strongly among forest strata and stand types. Douglas fir monocultures consistently supported lower taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic diversity at both local (plot) and regional (landscape) scales compared with the other stand types, with the most pronounced differences observed in the canopy. Mixture effects depended on the identity of admixed conifers: beech–spruce mixtures favoured beetle diversity on the forest floor, whereas beech–Douglas fir mixtures generally buffered canopy beetle diversity losses observed in Douglas fir monocultures. Canopy openness, deadwood volume and tree neighbourhood diversity shaped biodiversity across all strata. Subcanopy communities generally depended most on environmental features, while canopy communities were strongly driven by tree species identity. Community composition and feeding‐guild structure diverged with increasing stratum height, especially when comparing beech‐ and conifer‐dominated stands, underscoring the sensitivity of canopy assemblages to host tree identity due to their direct contact with tree‐specific habitats and resources. Synthesis and applications . Our findings emphasize the importance of integrating vertical stratification into biodiversity monitoring for a comprehensive understanding of the ecological impacts of climate‐adapted forest management with non‐native tree species. Promoting mixed stands can mitigate negative biodiversity impacts of non‐native tree species and support the maintenance of multidimensional biodiversity of associated forest biota under climate‐driven forest reorganization.
authors: Sara Piccini, Benjamin Wildermuth, Dragan Matevski, Peter Kriegel, Alice Penanhoat, Dominik Seidel, Jonas Hagge, Martin M. Gossner, Andreas Schuldt

title: Plant populations in ancient grasslands harbour higher levels of genetic diversity
abstract: Abstract Land‐use change and intensification can be a threat to biodiversity of grassland habitats, including genetic diversity. This is especially true for areas where drastic changes in land use occurred in recent years. The Allgäu in Germany is known for a large proportion of grassland in its landscape. However, the sites often differ in their current management intensity and their land use history. While some sites have been used as grasslands for more than two centuries, other grasslands are much younger. We assumed that landscape history and grassland management have a significant impact on genetic variation and therefore analysed the genetic variation of five typical grassland species using multiplexed ISSR (inter‐simple sequence repeat) genotyping by sequencing (MIG‐seq). We then related data on genetic variation with data on habitat quality, landscape structure and habitat age to identify possible drivers of genetic variation. Our results indicated a high level of gene flow across the study area. Consequently, genetic differentiation among populations was correlated with geographic distance. Genetic diversity clearly depended on habitat age but was not related to habitat conditions or landscape structure. Synthesis and applications . Since ancient grasslands harbour genetically more diverse plant populations, land use history should be given more attention in conservation management.
authors: Lena Winkler, Vinzenz Gilgenreiner, Hannah Schmitt, Christoph Reisch

title: Strategic dam management can offset climate‐driven declines in fish production
abstract: Abstract Climate change and hydrologic alteration by water infrastructure are reshaping river ecosystems globally, threatening freshwater biodiversity. Effective conservation strategies for riverine species depend on understanding how climate‐driven changes in temperature and flow interact with water management to regulate population dynamics, yet these interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we use a hierarchical Bayesian stock‐recruitment model to quantify how six decades of changing climate and water management (i.e. flow regulation at a large storage dam) jointly influence the productivity of 13 populations of a cold‐water fish species of significant conservation and economic importance, Yellowstone cutthroat trout ( Oncorhynchus virginalis bouvieri ) in the upper Snake River watershed, Wyoming, USA. We show that strong seasonal warming had opposing effects on productivity, with declines in warmer winters and springs but increases in warmer summers. The strongest driver of productivity was an interaction between the timing of natural and managed peak spring flows, where matched peak flow events reduced productivity, while mismatched peaks extended the flood pulse and increased productivity. In addition, key flow management periods, including summer irrigation flows and the timing of autumn ramp down, had important but smaller effects on productivity. Future climate projections indicated that continued warming and reduced spring flood duration may threaten trout productivity. However, our results show how adaptive dam management that strategically integrates with natural flow variability could offset climate‐driven declines and sustain ecosystem function. Synthesis and applications. Our results identify actionable levers for adaptive water management in the upper Snake River: delaying managed peak releases relative to natural flood peaks to extend the spring flood pulse, and postponing autumn ramp down to maintain side‐channel connectivity. While institutional constraints (e.g. water rights obligations) and hydrologic conditions (e.g. drought) may limit implementation, our findings provide key information for both long‐term and rapid‐response decision making. Quantifying the ecological value of water, as we do here, is essential for elevating fisheries and ecosystems services in water‐use negotiations dominated by consumptive demands. Our results provide a transferable framework for adaptive water management to support riverine biodiversity under intensifying warming and water scarcity.
authors: Jeffrey R. Baldock, Timothy J. Cline, William W. Fetzer, Annika Walters

title: Sea level rise weakens the restoration benefit of mussel–cordgrass facilitation in salt marshes
abstract: Abstract Ribbed mussels are ecosystem engineers that can enhance the performance of Spartina alterniflora and contribute to shoreline protection, but it remains unclear how mussel facilitation of cordgrass growth and associated stability benefits vary across inundation gradients expected under accelerating sea level rise. Identifying where this facilitation strengthens or weakens along the elevation gradient is, therefore, essential for anticipating restoration outcomes and designing interventions that leverage biotic interactions under future inundation regimes. We conducted a field mesocosm experiment on the Louisiana coast using marsh organs planted with S. alterniflora . We exposed the plants to five elevation treatments ( E = +5, 0, −5, −10 and −15 cm relative to the present marsh surface) to generate an inundation gradient spanning a low‐inundation hindcast, present‐day conditions and future relative elevation scenarios under sea level rise, and we crossed these elevations with four ribbed mussel ( Geukensia granosissima ) density treatments ( N = 0, 254, 509 and 1018 individuals m −2 ). Our results showed that mussel–cordgrass facilitation was strongly dependent on relative elevation: increasing mussel density enhanced plant biomass accumulation only within a distinct ‘facilitation window’ where elevation keeps pace with sea level rise (+5 to 0 cm relative elevation). At relative elevations of −5 cm and lower, the positive mussel–cordgrass interaction weakened rapidly, forming a ‘decoupling zone’. Structural equation modelling further suggested that greater realized mussel biomass was associated with higher soil organic matter and below‐ground biomass, whereas greater inundation frequency was associated with higher soil water content and lower soil organic matter and below‐ground biomass. Synthesis and applications. Within a limited elevation range near the present marsh surface, ribbed mussels facilitate S. alterniflora biomass accumulation; however, this facilitative interaction is contingent on relative elevation and is likely to weaken as relative elevation declines under future sea level rise. Consequently, relative elevation provides a practical screening metric for marsh restoration efforts, helping to prioritize locations for incorporating ribbed mussels where benefits to cordgrass biomass are most likely and to avoid settings where expected benefits are low. This screening metric can inform marsh restoration project siting, monitoring and adaptive management under future sea level rise.
authors: Yaolin Guo, Skylar L. Demourelle, Megan K. La Peyre, Brian J. Roberts

title: Correction to “High and dry: Environmental conditions drive opportunities for disease transmission in desert bighorn sheep”
abstract: Journal of Applied Ecology, Volume 63, Issue 7, July 2026.

title: Hotspots of tree richness and carbon storage in existing and potential protected areas in Mexico
abstract: Abstract Understanding the spatial relationship between biodiversity and carbon storage is essential for guiding conservation efforts to tackle jointly the biodiversity loss and climate change crises. Here, we assess tree richness and carbon storage patterns, their spatial congruence within and outside protected areas and to what extent existing protected areas safeguard tree diversity‐carbon storage hotspots. We used tree species richness and above‐ground carbon storage data derived from 234 national forest inventory plots to fit machine learning models using a set of climatic, topographic and edaphic predictors in northwestern Mexico. We then assessed the uncertainty and spatial congruence of predicted tree richness and carbon storage. Areas with high minimum temperature and evapotranspiration contain greater tree richness and carbon storage. These results suggest that changes in temperature and precipitation regimes have the potential to alter both plant diversity and carbon pools. Hotspots, where the top quintile values of tree richness and carbon storage overlap, occupy 10.2% of the study region; however, most lie beyond existing protected areas, which currently safeguard less than 0.2% of these hotspots. Synthesis and applications : We identified areas of potentially high conservation value, including prospective ecological reserves and corridors. We recommend policy makers and land managers to protect these hotspots of tree richness and carbon storage and establish connections with existing reserves to facilitate species movement and range expansion under changing climatic conditions. Biodiversity and carbon pools should be considered together for more effective spatial planning processes, especially at the regional scale, where management decisions can be more easily implemented and evaluated.
authors: Onésimo Galaz, Alejandro Cueva, Rafael A. Lara‐Reséndiz, Zulia M. Sánchez‐Mejía, Enrico A. Yépez, Jeannine Cavender‐Bares, Juan C. Álvarez‐Yépiz

title: Regulating bark beetles with mechanical bark treatments: Trade‐offs among pest control, operational efficiency and biodiversity
abstract: Abstract Natural disturbances have increasingly shaped global forests in recent decades. Coniferous forests in the Northern Hemisphere are facing intensifying disturbance regimes, exacerbating the conflict between traditional management objectives and the role of disturbance‐driven dynamics for biodiversity conservation. In Europe, unprecedented amounts of Norway spruce ( Picea abies ) have been damaged in recent years by hot droughts accompanied by outbreaks of the European Spruce Bark Beetle ( Ips typographus ). To meet the demands of forest protection and secure timber production, P. abies trees colonized by I. typographus , or suitable for colonization due to abiotic stress, are either extracted by salvage logging or made unsuitable for breeding using debarking techniques. Manual techniques are inefficient for large quantities and the extraction of deadwood can compromise biodiversity. We investigated mechanical bark treatments as potential alternatives to salvage logging for bark beetle regulation in Central Europe. Our study quantified bark beetle regulation efficacy, operational efficiency, wood properties and effects on biodiversity of saproxylic beetles, fungi and bacteria, as well as woodpeckers. Processing Norway spruce logs three times with a harvester to remove bark substantially reduced bark beetle emergence, demonstrating a scalable method that may contribute to the management of pest outbreaks and disturbances at landscape scales. Motor‐manual bark gouging and debarking are flexible alternatives and effective methods for small wood quantities. With increasing bark removal intensity, species richness of saproxylic beetles and bacteria decreased, while fungi species richness increased. In all three groups, species assemblages were affected by bark treatments. Differences in moisture content between treated and control logs were the main driver for changes in fungi and bacteria community assemblages. Bark treatments did not affect net calorific value over the first 2 years, blue‐stain fungi colonization and elemental composition (H, C and N). Synthesis and applications . Three times harvester processing and motor‐manual bark gouging effectively reduce bark beetles, enabling two options: permanent on‐site retention for biodiversity conservation, or up to 2 years of intermediate on‐site storage with no treatment effect on blue‐stain fungi colonization or energy content, thereby buffering operational bottlenecks during landscape disturbances.
authors: Sebastian Zarges, Peter Kriegel, Ole Henning, Andreas Schuldt, Simon Thorn, Jonas Hagge

title: A quantitative analysis to detect mass mortality events (wrecks) in Procellariiformes
abstract: Abstract Mass mortality events (MMEs) or ‘wrecks’ represent sudden and large‐scale mortality episodes often associated with extreme environmental conditions. Despite their ecological importance, MMEs remain poorly documented in the South Atlantic, particularly for Procellariiformes, a group highly vulnerable to climate‐driven anomalies. Detecting such events in this region is challenging because baseline mortality levels are unknown, limiting the ability of monitoring programs to identify abnormal mortality episodes. We developed a quantitative framework to detect and characterize seabird MMEs by integrating time‐series decomposition, changepoint analysis and kernel density estimation. The framework was applied to 8 years (2017–2024) of standardized beach monitoring data covering approximately 3320 km of the Brazilian coastline. This approach allowed us to identify anomalous mortality peaks, estimate the temporal duration of mortality episodes and delineate their spatial extent and hotspots along the coast. We detected seven previously unreported MMEs impacting 3779 stranded Procellariiformes. Events occurred primarily during austral autumn in northeastern and during austral spring in southeastern–southern regions, revealing recurrent seasonal and spatial patterns. Cory's Shearwater Calonectris borealis , Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus and Atlantic Yellow‐nosed Albatross Thalassarche chlororhynchos were the most affected species, with juveniles disproportionately represented. Kernel density analysis identified recurrent hotspot regions of mortality along the Brazilian coast. We propose mortality thresholds in an early‐warning system to guide monitoring efforts during abnormal stranding events. Synthesis and applications . Our study provides the first systematic assessment of seabird mass mortality events in the South Atlantic and introduces a transferable statistical framework for detecting MMEs in other taxa and regions lacking baseline mortality information. By identifying recurrent temporal anomalies, high‐risk areas and vulnerable species, we could establish quantitative indicators of MMEs. This approach offers a practical tool for monitoring programs to improve early detection of mortality events and to implement rapid response protocols.
authors: Laura Baes, Ana Carolina Ewbank, Henrique Chupil, Carolina Reigada

title: Do field margins matter more than floral resources? Arthropod activity and limited spillover of natural enemies from perennial flower strips into adjacent crops
abstract: Abstract The simplification of agricultural landscapes and widespread pesticide use are major drivers of biodiversity loss, particularly affecting beneficial arthropods that provide essential ecosystem services such as pollination and natural pest control. Flower strips have emerged as a promising agri‐environmental measure to mitigate these effects by offering floral resources, shelter and overwintering habitats. However, their effectiveness depends on multiple factors, including plant species composition, strip age, cutting regime, and the dispersal of natural enemies into adjacent crops. In a three‐year field study (2022–2024) in conventionally managed agricultural fields, we examined arthropod activity in perennial flower strips, control grass strips and adjacent crops (sugar beet and cereals). In spring, arthropods were sampled to assess overwintering success; in summer, we investigated arthropod activity with a focus on natural enemies and their dispersal from field margins into adjacent crops. Overall arthropod activity did not differ consistently between flower and grass strips; though certain natural enemy groups showed a preference for flower strips. A strong edge effect was observed, with arthropod activity consistently higher within strips and declining rapidly within 5 m into the crop. Spillover of natural enemies was comparable between flower and grass strips, though activity declined more sharply from five to 50 m from the grass strip in 2023 and 2024, suggesting a more sustained activity gradient near flower strips. Some groups showed higher activity densities at 5 m distances compared to 50 m distances indicating that a spillover from the margin exists but declines rapidly. Arthropod activity peaked in 2022, reflecting inter‐annual variability. Overwintering success was comparable in flower and grass strips, and overall increased from 2023 to 2024, the second and third years since strip establishment. Synthesis and applications . Both flower and grass strips supported significantly higher arthropod activity than adjacent crop fields, underlining the general ecological value of field margins regardless of floral composition. The observed group‐specific responses emphasize the need for taxa‐specific analyses within heterogeneous functional groups, rather than relying solely on aggregated patterns. While tailored flower strips can promote specific natural enemy groups and local arthropod conservation, their contribution to biological control is conditional on pest pressure and landscape context, temporally variable, and likely most effective in low‐input or organic systems where pesticide pressure does not suppress in‐field arthropod activity.
authors: Constanze Ohlendorf, Jörn Lehmhus, Christoph Joachim

title: Testing habitat suitability for seagrass restoration to inform future efforts in southwestern Australia
abstract: Abstract Coastal habitats underpin vital ecosystem services, yet urban and industrial expansion have driven widespread degradation, including extensive loss of seagrass meadows. With minimal natural recovery, effective seagrass restoration depends on targeting suitable habitats. Here, we assess a range of environmental factors to determine the drivers of habitat suitability in Cockburn Sound and Owen Anchorage, Perth, southwestern Australia, for future restoration efforts of the temperate foundational seagrass Posidonia australis . The region is a heavily industrialised port that has lost ~80% of its seagrass meadows and suffered ecosystem decline since the 1950–1960s. To test habitat suitability, 1536 P. australis sprigs were planted into twenty‐four 20.25m 2 plots across eight sites with differing environmental conditions and assessed over 18 months. Relationships between restoration success and biophysical processes from both in situ observations and modelled data (Cockburn Sound Integrated Ecosystem Model, CSIEM) were explored. Habitat suitability in the entire study area was further assessed by modelling Habitat Suitability Index (HSI) using the CSIEM output, based on established environmental requirements of the species, to identify areas with potential for future restoration. After 18 months, the average survival of P. australis transplants was 71.86%, however, this varied greatly between sites. Overall, we identified four well‐performing sites where shoot density showed a clear increase over time, three sites with moderate performance and one unsuccessful site. Many surviving transplants were producing new shoots after 6 months and, overall, leaf growth averaged 0.84 cm 2 shoot −1 day −1 . After exploring a wide range of site‐specific physical and biological traits (including sediment characteristics, light availability and hydrodynamic variables), the sites were grouped into clusters based on the environmental characteristics, showing that wave energy and turbulent oscillatory hydrodynamics are the major drivers of restoration success, followed by fouling and bioturbation. Synthesis and applications . Combining habitat suitability modelling with field‐based habitat assessment provides more precise inputs for mapping seagrass restoration suitability across regions and helps uncover the key drivers of restoration outcomes. This approach can greatly improve confidence in identifying the most suitable areas to maximise success in larger scale restoration efforts.
authors: Giulia Ferretto, Jennifer J. Verduin, Rachel Austin, Henry Evans, Matthew R. Hipsey, Peisheng Huang, Sherry Yi Zhai, Mike van Keulen, Gary A. Kendrick

title: Autumn inversion tillage reduces beneficial arthropods and delays their recovery into the following crop growing season
abstract: Abstract Effects of tillage in arable fields on taxonomic and functional responses of beneficial above‐ and below‐ground arthropod communities are poorly understood. We assessed arthropod communities in 30 conventionally managed crop fields in south‐western Sweden before and after autumn tillage. Treatments consisted of three levels of tillage intensity: inversion tillage, reduced tillage (non‐inversion) and no tillage (direct seeding). Reduced tillage and no tillage are considered conservation tillage practices. All fields were sown with winter cereals in autumn 2019, followed by winter oilseed rape sown in late summer 2020. Tillage occurred between cereal harvest and the sowing of winter oilseed rape. We measured soil mesofauna density, and density, taxonomic, compositional and functional diversity of ground‐dwelling predators. Inversion tillage decreased densities of above‐ and below‐ground beneficial arthropods. Conservation tillage resulted in higher species richness and lower community turnover following disturbance. Community compositional shifts following inversion tillage were characterised by lower community weighted mean (CWM) body size and reduced densities of carabids overwintering as imago in autumn, and higher spider CWM body size in spring, compared with conservation tillage treatments. Inversion tillage reduced spider density and richness throughout the following growing season, while soil mesofauna densities, carabid taxonomic diversity and functional composition recovered by spring. Synthesis and applications : Responses to tillage were taxon‐specific and likely depended on life‐stage and the dependency on structural habitat complexity. Management should balance trade‐offs between retaining local communities, meeting the needs of multiple taxa, and accounting for taxonomic and functional richness over time.
authors: Janina Heinen, Riccardo Bommarco, Maria Viketoft, Astrid Taylor, Ola Lundin, Sara E. Emery

title: Temporal and spatial trends in study designs used to understand what works in conservation
abstract: Abstract Robust study designs are essential for estimating the effects of conservation actions, but a range of evaluation designs are used that differ markedly in their robustness to bias. However, it is unclear whether robust designs are becoming more frequently used or how usage varies across subject areas and geographies. We analysed 7356 English and 1183 non‐English language primary studies that tested the effects of conservation actions from the Conservation Evidence database. We classified each study's methodological design to one of five broad types (After, Before–After [BA], Control–Impact [CI], Before–After–Control–Impact [BACI] and randomised experiments) and fitted a Bayesian multinomial logistic regression, with study‐level random effects, to test how design usage varies by year, national income, biodiversity intactness, language and subject area. The evidence base has shifted gradually from dominance by simple After designs (1970–2023: 74% to 33%) towards greater use of CI (15% to 39%) and more robust designs: randomised experiments (0% to 15%) and BACI (1% to 6%). Design use was uneven across subjects, with randomised experiments more common in habitat and soil‐focused topics (e.g. farmland), and After or BA designs more common in animal‐focused topics (e.g. birds and reptiles). Studies in non‐English languages and lower‐income countries were more likely to use After and BA designs and less likely to use randomised experiments and CI designs. Geographical coverage of robust designs was limited: randomised experiments and BACI studies occurred in few countries, and many biodiverse and environmentally degraded countries had few or no evaluations using any design. Despite modest improvements over time, several structural and contextual constraints (linked to subject, language and resources) continue to shape where rigorous evaluation is feasible. Synthesis and applications : Conservation is shifting towards using more robust designs to evaluate actions, but these remain rare. We suggest embedding study design choice more strategically within adaptive management and evidence‐based conservation practice, encouraging cost‐efficient, context‐dependent upgrades to more robust designs. This will require targeted capacity building, researcher–practitioner partnerships and longer‐term funding—especially in biodiverse, lower‐income countries with few studies of any design, let alone more robust ones.
authors: Amelia Staples, William H. Morgan, Lynn V. Dicks, Silviu O. Petrovan, Rebecca K. Smith, William J. Sutherland, Alec P. Christie

title: Designing effective oral rabies vaccination strategies for endangered carnivores: Lessons from bait uptake in Ethiopian wolves
abstract: Abstract Effective disease control is vital in mitigating devastating disease outbreaks among threatened wild animal populations living in proximity to domestic animal reservoir populations. With only ~500 individuals remaining in small, isolated populations in the Ethiopian highlands, the most immediate threat to endangered Ethiopian wolves Canis simensis is rabies transmission from nearby domestic dogs Canis familiaris . Since 2018, the Ethiopian Wolf Conservation Programme (EWCP) has conducted oral vaccinations of Ethiopian wolves to control rabies spread. Analysis of camera trap images from 580 bait stations across five Ethiopian wolf populations between 2018 and 2020 enabled species uptake to be confirmed for 416 baits. Ethiopian wolves were the main bait consumers (46%), with peak uptake occurring soon after deployment in the evening. Non‐target uptake was almost exclusively diurnal, and predominantly by rodents, birds of prey and domestic dogs (41%). Generalised linear models showed that location and vegetation type influenced bait uptake by Ethiopian wolves and indicated that interference competition with domestic dogs can reduce Ethiopian wolf bait uptake near human settlements and where dogs are more active during the day. Synthesis and application: Our methods and framework offer valuable insights for designing effective oral vaccination strategies in wild carnivores globally, especially where domestic animal interference threatens wildlife health interventions.
authors: Elizabeth Fiona Rosemary Preston, Jessica Chalkley, Muktar Abute, Alo Hussein, Eric Bedin, Jorgelina Marino

title: Insecticides alter wild and managed pollination dynamics on oil crop yield
abstract: Abstract Global production of Ethiopian rape ( Brassica carinata ) is increasing for biofuel and feed purposes, yet its pollination ecology remains poorly understood despite its similarity to other mass‐flowering Brassica crops. We experimentally investigated how floral resource availability, insecticide use, and managed honey bee hives interact to shape pollination and yield at different scales. We conducted a 2‐year field experiment across 35 sites in the Northern Great Plains, USA, monitoring over 800 focal plants. We quantified pollinator visitation, diversity, movement, flower traits, and seed set across plant, field, and site scales, and assessed how insecticide application altered pollinator behaviour and crop performance. Pollinators increased seed set by 26.8%, with 28 visiting species recorded. Wild pollinators were more efficient than honey bees, contributing 1.01 seeds per visit compared with 0.79. In pesticide‐free fields, interactions between wild and managed pollinators produced non‐additive effects, suggesting context‐dependent competition and facilitation. In contrast, insecticide application disproportionately reduced wild pollinators, while honey bees partially compensated, buffering yield losses. However, wild pollinators consistently delivered higher per‐visit efficiency across spatial scales, although this advantage declined under chemical exposure. Synthesis and applications . Our results show that combining honey bee hives with insecticide use does not automatically enhance crop yield. Pollination outcomes are strongly scale‐ and context‐dependent, with wild pollinators providing disproportionately important services. Agricultural management should therefore prioritize integrated strategies that reduce pesticide pressure, enhance habitat, and support wild pollinator diversity to maintain resilient pollination services in intensive agroecosystems.
authors: Henning Nottebrock, Shane Stiles, Alexandra‐Maria Klein, Jonathan G. Lundgren, Charles B. Fenster

title: eDNA sampling reveals no evidence of negative effects of beaver recolonisation on the catchment‐scale distribution of migratory fish
abstract: Abstract Reintroduction of keystone species is considered part of the solution to the current biodiversity crisis. The Eurasian beaver ( Castor fiber ) is one such species, shaping its habitat by felling trees, building dams and creating wetlands. However, whilst the potential benefits to aquatic biodiversity and ecological functioning have been studied on a local scale, the impacts of beavers on catchment‐scale processes such as fish migration remain understudied. Sequencing of environmental DNA (eDNA metabarcoding) from water samples is a cost‐effective method to study species distributions across large geographical scales. Here, eDNA samples ( n = 426) were collected from 142 sites across Britain's oldest and largest established wild beaver population, located on Tayside, East Scotland and analysed using a vertebrate‐specific metabarcoding assay. We combined detection/non‐detection data from eDNA results with other environmental and anthropogenic variables to model the effects of beaver eDNA detections on the distribution of three migratory fish species. Using generalised linear models, we found no effects of the current beaver eDNA detections on the distribution of Atlantic salmon or lamprey, but a positive co‐occurrence with European eel at the catchment scale. Model outputs also reinforced previous findings on the impact of barriers to migration and other abiotic and biotic factors on fish species, demonstrating the effectiveness of eDNA sampling in rivers for understanding species distributions at a catchment scale. Synthesis and applications . This study provides novel insights into the catchment‐scale co‐distribution of beavers and migratory fish, and there was no evidence of negative effects on the catchment‐scale distribution of migratory fish species. More generally, this study highlights how catchment‐wide eDNA monitoring can be applied by environmental managers to aid decision‐making and impact assessment of multiple priority species at the catchment scale.
authors: James A. Macarthur, Alan Law, Nigel J. Willby, Dasha Svobodova, Nathan P. Griffiths, Roo D. Campbell, Martin J. Gaywood, Colin W. Bean, Lori Lawson Handley, Melanie Smith, Shaun Leonard, Chris Conroy, Victoria L. Pritchard, Bernd Hänfling

title: Mangrove expansion in a large river delta is dependent on foreshore geomorphology
abstract: Abstract Understanding the environmental conditions facilitating mangrove expansion across the large scale of entire deltas or estuaries (~100 to 1000 km 2 ) remains limited, despite its relevance for upscaling mangrove restoration strategies, which necessitates knowledge on where active planting of mangrove seedlings has a high versus low chance of success. In this study, we investigate the environmental conditions facilitating mangrove development across the Guayas Delta in Ecuador, a large tropical river delta (~ 3200 km 2 ) where young mangrove forests are expanding across extensive intertidal mudflats. By combining satellite‐based remote‐sensing, drone‐based field verification and statistical modelling, we quantified differences in environmental conditions between mudflats showing active mangrove expansion versus mudflats with stable mangrove edges. We analysed key variables, including mudflat elevation, slope, curvature, wind fetch, mudflat length and tidal inundation duration, frequency and depth. Our results reveal that the morphology of the tidal flat foreshore is a key determinant of mangrove edge dynamics, and a stronger predictor than more commonly used inundation metrics such as the elevation, inundation duration, frequency and depth at the mangrove edge. In general, mangrove expansion is facilitated by wide foreshores that have low slopes and straight profile shapes, which are attributed to more efficient attenuation of waves and tidal currents. Conversely, mangroves are much less likely to expand when they border narrow, steeper and concave foreshores that provide minimal protection and that occur at lower intertidal elevations, where they experience increased inundation stress. Synthesis and applications . Our findings provide guidance for large‐scale mangrove restoration, particularly in tropical river deltas, by identifying sites where (1) mangroves can potentially expand in the future, and (2) conditions are favourable for active mangrove seedling planting. The presence of a mudflat in front of existing mangroves is not sufficient. Instead, mangrove planting should be prioritized on mudflats with low tidal inundation stress, low slope, large width and convex topographic profiles, while low intertidal areas with narrow, steep and concave mudflat foreshores should be avoided. These specific geomorphic mudflat characteristics may serve as indicators to select suitable mangrove planting sites at a large deltaic scale.
authors: Maria‐Esther Espinoza‐Celi, Jean‐Philippe Belliard, Gregory S. Fivash, Luis Dominguez‐Granda, Ignace Pelckmans, John Ramos‐Veliz, Jorge Peñaherrera, Stijn Temmerman

title: A global systematic review of the effects of hydromorphological floodplain restoration on biodiversity
abstract: Abstract River floodplains are among the most threatened ecosystems on Earth. Efforts at hydromorphological restoration by enhancing lateral connectivity between the river channel and former floodplain are increasingly popular as nature‐based solutions (NbS) for hydrometeorological risk, including flood management and drought resilience, while potentially improving habitat for fish and wildlife and performing other ecosystem services. However, the biodiversity conservation benefits of such interventions have not been comprehensively assessed. A comprehensive review of hydromorphological floodplain restorations and their conservation evidence is needed to guide managers in selecting interventions and understanding potential outcomes. Here we report findings from a systematic review of 100 studies monitoring ecological responses to hydromorphological floodplain restoration across 22 countries from four continents and a broad range of taxonomic groups including birds, fishes, invertebrates, plants and amphibians. Most research comes from temperate climates, especially in Europe, and assesses restoration success at local scales by comparing restored to reference sites, with less than 20% of studies using a full Before‐After‐Control‐Impact (BACI) Design. The most common interventions used were side‐channel excavation, lowering of the floodplain, levee setbacks and environmental flows, and these yielded generally positive effects on metrics of biodiversity. Studies showed variation in biodiversity response among river systems, intervention types, spatiotemporal scales and among taxonomic groups. Studies were biased towards invertebrates, plants and fish, with little research on terrestrial vertebrates (birds, amphibians, and small mammals, including bats) and soil microorganisms. Synthesis and applications . Our evidence synthesis reinforces the notion that hydromorphological floodplain restorations, as a biodiversity conservation measure or NbS, can significantly enhance local floodplain biodiversity. However, such benefits were often compromised at least in part by invasive species post‐restoration, highlighting the importance of sustained management.
authors: Rabindra Parajuli, Mark D. Dixon, Annie Blalock, Aurora Fowler, Sandesh Sigdel, Kimberly I. Magnuson, Seth J. Wenger, Burton Suedel, David J. Crane, Charles B. van Rees

title: Integrating large mammalian herbivores into Dynamic Global Vegetation Models: Status and next steps
abstract: Abstract Zoogeochemistry, the study of how animals influence elemental cycling within ecosystems, bridges the fields of zoology, ecology and biogeochemistry. Yet, most terrestrial ecosystem models, especially Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs), remain largely plant‐centric and rarely capture animal‐driven feedbacks. This omission could lead to misrepresentation of carbon and nutrient cycling, which is particularly pertinent at a time of continued widespread defaunation but also animal introductions (trophic rewilding) gaining traction as a potential mitigation measure. Here, we review global evidence from field observations, experimental manipulations, remote sensing and modelling to understand how animals, influence carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycling through consumption (e.g. herbivory), transformation and redistribution (via faeces, urine and carcasses) and physical disturbances (e.g. trampling). While zoogeochemistry encompasses all animals, this review focuses primarily on terrestrial vertebrates, particularly large mammals. We then trace the historical development of how animals have been represented in contemporary DGVMs, beginning with implicit representations and progressing towards explicit representations. Persistent gaps remain in capturing key animal‐driven processes, and relating these to functional traits (body size, foraging strategy, etc.), mammal‐mediated biogeochemical cycling, animal–microbial interactions and in development of adequate model validation approaches. To address these challenges, we propose a modular framework guided by the principle of ‘complexity by necessity,’ which links trait‐based animal cohorts to above‐ and below‐ground processes through consumption, defecation and other animal‐driven inputs, capturing spatial behaviours, plant–microbe–soil interactions and predator–prey dynamics across scales. Integrating zoogeochemical mechanisms into DGVMs would replace the traditional black‐box approach to animal processes with explicit mechanistic modelling. This offers a process‐based tool to quantify local animal impacts, scale across large regions and rigorously evaluate the expected outcomes for ecosystem structure and biogeochemistry. In the future, we call for better implementation of animal interactions and habitat‐mediated feedbacks, such as behavioural effects through predation or fear (predator–prey interactions). To more accurately simulate the nutrient cycling in soil, we suggest expanding models to include interactions with soil‐engineering invertebrates and larger animals. Collectively, these improvements would advance our mechanistic understanding of animal‐driven biogeochemistry and their importance for predicting nutrient cycles and animal–plant–soil feedbacks within Earth system models. authors: Yue Cheng, Joanne Alice O'Keeffe, Andrew J. Abraham, Jesper Riis Christiansen, Frederik Nygaard Philipsen, Klaus Steenberg Larsen, Fabio Berzaghi, Carsten W. Mueller, Lars Vesterdal, Jeppe A. Kristensen, Elizabeth Le Roux

title: Trait responses to competition are mostly parallel among competitor plants but can cause convergence or divergence in key traits
abstract: Abstract Plants competing for resources exhibit different traits than plants which are not. Phenotypic plasticity can shape competition by altering trait differences between competitors. Studies show that plastic traits may converge or diverge among competitors as competition intensifies. However, another possibility is that interacting species could exhibit similar trait shifts as competition intensifies (trait parallelism). We used a field experiment to assess trait responses and performance outcomes for six co‐occurring native and invasive annual California grassland species when grown together at various densities. We grew one focal individual of each species in each plot and manipulated the identity and density of competitors, from bare ground to a dense lawn. Species displayed many trait responses to competitor density, which depended on competitor identity more than focal species identity. Most trait responses were parallel among competing plants with no effect on trait differences between competitors. The exceptions were specific root length, which diverged among competitors with increased competitor density, root mass fraction and leaf dry matter content, which both converged among competitors with increased competitor density. Competitors' effects on performance were not correlated with greater responses in any trait. A few traits displayed non‐parallel responses among competing plants, altering trait differences between competitors. These traits may be of interest for future studies of plasticity's effects on competition or species coexistence. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.
authors: Julia Bebout, Juliana Loaiza, Alexander Gillert, Elsa Cleland

title: Bridging the divide between models of animal‐driven and microbial‐driven biogeochemical cycling: A zoogeochemistry‐informed framework
abstract: Abstract Most current terrestrial biogeochemical models formalize biogeochemical cycling as predominantly controlled by processes involving plants and soil microbes. However, growing evidence indicates that above‐ground animals could exert controlling feedback effects that alter soil microbial performance via trophic interactions on plants, release of chemicals in waste matter deposition, and biophysical impacts on soil properties. We present a conceptual and mathematical framework—a Coupled Aboveground‐Belowground Zoogeochemical (CAB–ZGC) cycling model—that explicitly links above‐ground animal direct and feedback effects in models of below‐ground processes. We then provide an empirical synthesis, informed by the conceptual framework, to quantify the potential direction and magnitude of vertebrate and invertebrate animal impacts on below‐ground microbial processes. The synthesis of 39 studies provides proof‐of‐concept showing that animal presence can alter key biogeochemical processes including soil nutrient availability for microbes, microbial and fungal activity, microbial litter processing, and carbon and nitrogen cycling by between 10% to 219% relative to their absence. Effects were enhancing in 65% of cases, and reducing in 35%, and invertebrate density was a strong predictor of the effect and magnitude for microbial activity and nitrogen cycling. These findings reveal the importance of considering animal effects in biogeochemical models to improve the accuracy of model predictions and empirical assessments of biogeochemical cycling in ecosystems. We conclude by highlighting two complementary research fronts to advance terrestrial biogeochemical models: (i) model development through case studies to build a more general CAB‐ZGS model and (ii) target empirical work to measure animal parameters including flux rates, forage intake, animal respiration and waste across a range of animal densities and contexts. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.
authors: Janey R. Lienau, Nathalie R. Sommer, Oswald J. Schmitz

title: Reduction in litter allelochemicals promotes positive biotic interactions among alien species
abstract: Abstract A key focus of invasion ecology is elucidating why multiple alien species accumulate within ecosystems. The invasional meltdown hypothesis proposes that one alien invader promotes further invasions through soil legacy effects. However, whether microbial or litter legacies drive these effects, both of which are shaped by environmental heterogeneity (e.g., alien density or nutrient gradients), remains largely unexplored. We conducted a multifactorial experiment using an invasive plant species ( Phytolacca americana ) to assess how species origin affects alien plant invasion, incorporating two interacting species origins (native vs. alien), two litter treatments (with vs. without), two soil microbial conditions (inoculated vs. sterile), three soil phosphorus levels, and three planting density levels. Alien litter had lower total phenolic levels and higher C:N ratios than native litter. Phytolacca americana grew significantly better under alien litter. Path analysis revealed that this growth enhancement was driven primarily by reduced allelochemicals rather than nutrient differences, with plant density modulating this effect. Although soil microbial communities from different origins differed in diversity and functional structure, their inoculation produced no significant differential effects on P. americana growth. These results reveal a litter‐mediated mechanism that could potentially facilitate invasional meltdown by promoting positive interactions among alien plants. Our findings provide new insights into invasion mechanisms and highlight the ecological interplay between alien species. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.
authors: Yunhao Meng, Yanhui Zhuge, Xinze Geng, Ping Zhu, Guangyan Ni, Lori Daniels, Xinfu Bai, Shuxian Wang, Zhaolei Qu, Ping Zhang, Yuping Hou

title: Ecohydrological characteristics of biocrusts explain divergent responses of biocrusts and grasses to rainfall reduction
abstract: Abstract Drylands are mainly structured by both vascular plants and biological soil crusts (biocrusts), the latter often regarded as a self‐organizing component of these ecosystems. Yet how the covers of these two components respond jointly to rainfall variability remains unclear—a critical gap for predicting future dryland resilience and carbon–water dynamics. To that end, we conducted a 4‐year rainfall reduction experiment (−75%, −50%, −25% and control) in a semi‐arid grassland with a large number of replicates, allowing a robust assessment of ecosystem responses under natural conditions. We found that grass cover responded mainly to rainfall reduction treatments, showing consistent declines due to their dependence on water input. Biocrust cover was more resilient to rainfall reduction but strongly promoted by years with more frequent rainfall events, reflecting their poikilohydric nature. Ecohydrological characteristics of biocrusts—specifically their rainfall thresholds for minimum carbon gain (carbon‐balancing rainfall size) and maximum water absorption (maximum usable rainfall size)—explained these divergent responses by mediating water availability. Synthesis . Our findings show that biocrusts mediate grass water supply by intercepting a significant fraction of rainfall; failing to account for this hydrological interaction leads to a biased overestimate of plant‐available water. This underscores the need to integrate biocrust‐plant interactions into experimental and modelling frameworks to improve predictions of dryland ecosystem sustainability under climate change. authors: Haoran Luo, Jiamin Shi, Qianhai Ye, Siqing Wang, Li Ma, Yali Ma, Linjie Qiao, Renyi Zhang, Yunyao Ma, Hao Wang, Xiaobo Yuan, Chao Song, Changming Zhao, Ning Chen

title: Facilitation and competition between Acacia species and phosphorus‐mobilising plants in severely phosphorus‐impoverished habitats
abstract: Abstract Plants in fire‐prone severely phosphorus (P)‐impoverished environments exhibit diverse P‐acquisition strategies coordinated with root morphological traits. Fire transiently enhances plant‐available soil P, making efficient post‐fire P acquisition crucial for seedling survival of post‐fire seeder perennials as soil P availability declines over time. However, whether post‐fire seeder perennials express a diversity of P‐acquisition strategies across three stages of seedlings after a fire and how their root morphological traits are coordinated, remains unknown. For Acacia pulchella and Acacia lasiocarpa (Fabaceae), two post‐fire seeder perennials native to southwest Australian P‐impoverished habitats, we investigated biomass, rhizosheath monophosphatase activity and carboxylate concentrations, represented by leaf manganese concentrations ([Mn]), leaf P‐resorption efficiency and root morphological traits. Seedlings were harvested at three stages in monoculture and mixture with P‐mobilising Banksia species (Proteaceae), under treatments with or without P addition to simulate soil P concentrations ([P]) immediately and many years post‐fire, respectively. The two species of Acacia exhibited distinct P‐acquisition strategies. A. pulchella initially relied on increased soil P availability and subsequently its P acquisition was facilitated by Banksia attenuata ( B. attenuata ), while consistently depending on releasing monophosphatases. Conversely, A. lasiocarpa relied on releasing carboxylates and monophosphatases to mobilise and acquire P, even at elevated soil [P]. There were efficiency interactions among root morphological traits, rhizosheath monophosphatases, leaf [Mn] and leaf P‐resorption efficiency. For both Acacia species, total biomass was most strongly predicted by root morphological traits. We conclude that traits related to the acquisition of soil P, such as root morphological characteristics, rhizosheath monophosphatases and leaf [Mn] were more evident in supporting plant growth in severely P‐impoverished ecosystems than traits associated with internal P conservation, such as leaf P‐resorption efficiency. These two types of traits interacted and functioned synergistically, enhancing total plant biomass. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.
authors: Ling‐Ling Chen, Zhao Zhang, Qi Shen, Joanna Kotula, Shu Tong Liu, Patrick M. Finnegan, Kosala Ranathunge, Hans Lambers

title: Elevated CO2 advances vegetation phenology
abstract: Abstract The continuous rise in atmospheric CO 2 concentration has profoundly altered vegetation structure and function across terrestrial ecosystems. Among various indicators, vegetation phenology is conventionally considered an early warning indicator of changes in other ecosystem processes. However, the relationship between vegetation phenology and elevated CO 2 (eCO 2 ) remains highly elusive. Here, we conducted a comprehensive meta‐analysis of 624 experimental records from 39 published studies to evaluate eCO 2 effects on vegetation phenology and quantify the relative importance of climate variables, soil factors, eCO 2 magnitude and experimental duration. The findings showed that eCO 2 significantly advanced overall vegetation phenology by 2.50 days (−1.99%), with leaf‐out advancing by 3.00 days (−2.38%) and maturity by 4.09 days (−3.24%). Elevated CO 2 exerted a negligible overall effect on plant growing season length. Importantly, model selection showed that plant functional groups were not essential predictors of phenological shifts. Instead, phenological shifts were primarily predicted by mean annual temperature (MAT) and eCO 2 magnitude. These results provide new insights into the mechanisms linking atmospheric change with plant developmental timing and highlight the need to explicitly incorporate CO 2 ‐driven phenological responses into ecosystem and Earth system models. authors: Yuanyi Gao, Lin Ma, Guang Zhao, Hua Liu, Qingyang Rao, Yanmin Teng, Yanzhen Hou, Haojie Guo, Jing Zhao, Xiaolin Sun, Xinyu Guo, Ziyang Peng, Yangjian Zhang

title: Elevated UV‐B alters anti‐herbivore plant defence allocation, while silicon supplementation maintains resistance
abstract: Abstract The impacts of elevated surface ultraviolet‐B (UV‐B) on ecological processes, such as anti‐herbivore defence in plants, remain poorly understood. Many cereal crops depend on accumulating silicon (Si) in their tissues to resist insect herbivory. UV‐B is known to affect oxidative signalling, which is an early signal triggered by herbivore attack and hence could potentially impact upon subsequent defence allocation. We tested how UV‐B light, Si supplementation and herbivory interact to impact plant defence and insect performance. We conducted a fully factorial glasshouse experiment using hydroponically grown wheat ( Triticum aestivum ), manipulating three UV‐B levels (low, moderate and high) and Si supply, before subjecting plants to herbivory by Helicoverpa armigera . Elevated UV‐B increased oxidative signalling (+52%) and antioxidant capacity but slightly reduced foliar Si accumulation (−8.6%). Silicon supplementation reduced lipid peroxidation and altered defence allocation, lowering UV‐B‐ and herbivory‐induced phenolic production while increasing polyphenol oxidase activity and Si concentration. Phenolics increased under elevated UV‐B (up to +13%), and herbivory increased phenolics only in plants without Si supplementation (up to +30%). Under herbivory, Si reduced phenolic levels (17% lower than −Si plants) and suppressed phenolic induction by 25%. Larvae feeding on Si‐supplemented plants showed a 35% reduction in growth rate, which persisted despite UV‐B‐driven reductions in foliar Si. High UV‐B depleted larval energy reserves, with carbohydrate levels declining by 52%, alongside reduced lipid and triglyceride stores and a 40% increase in protein. Silicon altered larval energy allocation, increasing carbohydrate reserves (2.5‐fold) and glycogen (up to 2.9‐fold), while larvae feeding on −Si plants retained higher lipid and triglyceride stores. Collectively, these results demonstrate that Si helps maintain plant resistance under simultaneous UV‐B exposure and herbivory by altering defence investment and increasing metabolic costs to herbivores. These findings provide broader implications for understanding how crops maintain resistance under future changes in UV‐B light conditions. authors: Sajjad Reyhani Haghighi, Christopher I. Cazzonelli, Sue E. Hartley, Scott N. Johnson

title: Bio‐organic fertilizer alleviated soil microbial C limitations, aggravated P limitations and increased microbial C use efficiency in a degraded desert steppe
abstract: Abstract Bio‐organic fertilizer (BOF), which integrates organic carbon sources, beneficial microorganisms and essential nutrients, represents a distinctive approach to grassland restoration that differs fundamentally from conventional fertilization practices. Ecoenzymatic stoichiometry theory (EEST) provides a powerful framework for evaluating microbial nutrient limitation and carbon use efficiency (CUE) via analysis of the metabolic activities of extracellular enzymes involved in nutrient acquisition, supporting research on their responses to carbon‐rich amendments and informing the optimization of restoration strategies. In this study, we investigated the responses of microbial metabolic limitations and CUE to different ecological restoration measures: bio‐organic fertilizer (BOF), microbial fertilizer (MF), super absorbent polymers (SAP) and a natural restoration control (CK). We quantified microbial metabolic limitation using three soil enzyme stoichiometry models (vector model, vector‐TER (threshold element ratio) (V–T) model and threshold model), calculated microbial CUE across all treatments and examined the regulatory effects of environmental factors on both microbial metabolic nutrient limitations and CUE. Different restoration measures significantly affected soil physicochemical properties, microbial biomass, extracellular enzyme activities and their stoichiometric characteristics. All three restoration measures altered stoichiometric imbalance: compared with CK, BOF, MF and SAP treatments exhibited higher C:N imbalance but lower C:P and N:P imbalances. All three models consistently indicated the absence of soil microbial N limitation across all restoration measures, with all three models confirming the presence of C and P limitations. Both vector and V–T models showed that BOF alleviated C limitations with no significant differences in P limitations among treatments, whereas the threshold model revealed that BOF relieved C limitations but exacerbated P limitations. Additionally, BOF improved CUE. The main factors that influenced C and P limitations were soil available resources. Meanwhile, soil microbial biomass was the main factor influencing CUE. This study demonstrates the utility of EEST in elucidating microbial resource ecology in degraded desert grasslands, providing a basis for targeted restoration measures in degraded ecosystems. authors: Yao Zhou, Wen Li, Jing Ma, Jinzhen Li, Haixin Jiang, Guohui Wang, Yan Shen, Hongbin Ma

title: Life history attributes influencing metabolic variation in an estuarine fish
abstract: Abstract Considering that energy availability and oxygen transport potential are limited in supplying metabolic requirements, all animals face trade‐offs between competing metabolic demands. A key interest of eco‐physiologists is to understand these trade‐offs and determine which strategies might prove the most efficient in the face of environmental challenges like climate warming. Here, we analysed three large datasets on a diadromous fish species, Galaxias maculatus, to assess metabolic rates of juveniles and reproductive adults across four acclimation temperatures (15, 18, 20 and 23°C). We used natural variations in growth rate and reproductive maturation level between and within individuals at different life history stages to test for potential relationships with different levels of aerobic metabolism from resting (standard metabolic rate, SMR) to maximal (maximum metabolic rate, MMR) We found that allometry of SMR differed predictably with warming temperature, whereby the intercept (scaling coefficient) increased and the slope (scaling exponent) decreased. This was driven by a trend in which the SMR of larger fish was less responsive to temperature relative to smaller fish. MMR allometry showed differences in intercept, but negligible differences in slope with temperature. Linear regression analyses on mass‐standardized variables showed individual growth phenotypes have a weak positive correlation with SMR at some, but not all, temperatures. This suggests that SMR may be a contributing determinant of growth, or the measurement of SMR could be impacted by residual growth even when fish have been fasted. No correlation between individual growth and MMR was seen at any temperature. We found a reduction in the number of individuals that reproductively matured at the lowest and highest temperatures. While there was no discernible correlation between the level of reproductive maturation and SMR, a paired t ‐test on a subset of fish showed that SMR was significantly lower in individuals when they were mature relative to when they were immature. There was also a negative relationship between maturation and MMR at 18°C, raising questions around the whole‐animal metabolic consequences of allocating energy to reproduction. We suggest that metabolism, growth and reproductive investment may not trade‐off as clearly as theory predicts, and we propose future research directions to untangle the complicated balance of these traits for maximizing lifetime fitness under a changing climate. authors: Elizabeth C. Hoots, Luis L. Kuchenmüller, Michael R. Skeeles, Timothy D. Clark

title: Intraspecific variability in feather moult extent declines under both low and high constraints
abstract: Abstract Intraspecific trait variability (ITV) is a fundamental feature of biological populations and the raw material upon which natural selection acts, yet its drivers remain poorly understood. We examined how environmental and intrinsic constraints shape ITV in a key avian morphological trait—the extent of feather moult—which directly affects an individual's future appearance, and thus its attractiveness, competitive ability, and overall fitness. Using data from 21,050 individuals across 219 passerine species, collected through fieldwork and from zoological collections, we quantified variation in the extent of feather replacement during post‐juvenile and pre‐breeding moults and developed a time extremity index (TEx) representing the degree of constraint on the time available for feather renewal. Phylogenetic models revealed that ITV in moult extent declined when TEx values were high, corresponding to either highly constrained or highly permissive conditions, and peaked at low TEx values, representing intermediate conditions, with stronger effects observed in post‐juvenile than in pre‐breeding moult. These results demonstrate that extreme environmental or life history constraints limit individual responses and reduce phenotypic variability, while intermediate conditions foster greater diversity in moult patterns and trait expression. This pattern suggests that moderate environmental pressures allow for the coexistence of multiple adaptive solutions within populations, enhancing ecological flexibility. Our findings provide empirical evidence for an extremity‐dependent association between environmental constraints and intraspecific variation, emphasizing that variability itself is context‐dependent. This pattern may help explain why populations facing moderate, rather than extreme, ecological pressures often display the highest potential for morphological flexibility and adaptive diversity. title: The negative effects of an allelopathic invader on native plant photosynthesis are amplified after tree canopy closure
abstract: Abstract Many invasive plants produce antimicrobial allelopathic compounds that disrupt plant–fungal symbioses of native species in the communities they invade, influencing nutrient and water provisioning that support photosynthesis. Previous studies have linked these disruptions to reductions in photosynthesis and stomatal conductance, but whether these effects are tied to reductions in photosynthetic capacity remains unclear, limiting inferences about the mechanisms driving physiological responses of native species. Furthermore, how these responses vary temporally across the growing season is unknown. To investigate the temporal dynamics of native plant responses to allelopathic invasion, we measured gas exchange in two understory native species ( Trillium spp. and Maianthemum racemosum ) at two points during the growing season—before and after tree canopy closure. Plants were measured in a long‐term field experiment where Alliaria petiolata , an allelopathic invader known to disrupt AM fungal symbioses, has been removed or left at ambient levels since 2006. Both native species exhibited significantly reduced net photosynthesis rates under ambient A. petiolata levels compared with the weeded treatment. This response was due to a reduction in apparent photosynthetic capacity in Trillium spp. and a reduction in stomatal conductance that increased stomatal limitation in M. racemosum . Photosynthetic responses to A. petiolata in both species were amplified after tree canopy closure. Alliaria petiolata reduced native plant net photosynthesis either by increasing nutrient stress, as indicated by the reduction in apparent photosynthetic capacity ( Trillium spp.), or by increasing water stress, as indicated by the reduction in stomatal conductance ( M. racemosum ). These responses were amplified only after the tree canopy closed. Our findings highlight the importance of seasonal changes that can regulate plant physiological responses to allelopathic invaders and demonstrate the diversity of mechanisms by which allelopathic invaders can influence native plant physiology.
